The fierce writer of biblical prose spent most of his first four decades anchored to Tennessee, a child of Appalachia with a lilting drawl and a regional outlook. By the early 1970s, he had published three Faulknerian novels—none of which sold well—and was struggling to finish a fourth book that aimed to chronicle his hometown of Knoxville in the way James Joyce had written about Dublin. McCarthy’s pockets were empty and his second marriage was failing. His then-wife, Annie DeLisle, recalled that on New Year’s Eve 1973, the year he turned 40, he suddenly announced that it was time for a change. As a friend put it, “He just walked off and left everything except his boots and his typewriter.” Pointing his truck west on I-40, McCarthy started driving and spent time in Tucson; Santa Fe; and Juárez, Mexico, before settling in El Paso, where he began researching a new novel called Blood Meridian . Few life swerves are so productive. The book represented a fresh direction. Instead of another story set in the forests and shambling urban peripheries of Appalachia, Blood Meridian (1985) was an epic Western. It ambitiously set out to align the nation’s past with humankind’s age-old thirst for violence: Wolves cull one another, and so do people. From then on, the fearsome stakes of the West—territorial competition, crime, blood, death—defined McCarthy’s fiction and yielded his strongest work. manifest.summaryEvidence: To understand Cormac McCarthy’s midlife crisis, look at America’s landscape. The fierce writer of biblical prose spent most of his first four decades anchored to Tennessee, a child of Appalachia with a lilting drawl and a regional outlook. By the early 1970s, he had published three Faulknerian novels—none of which sold well—and was struggling to finish a fourth book that aimed to chronicle his hometown of Knoxville in the way James Joyce had written about Dublin. McCarthy’s pockets were empty and his second marriage was failing. His then-wife, Annie DeLisle, recalled that on New Year’s Eve 1973, the year he turned 40, he suddenly announced that it was time for a change. As a friend put it, “He just walked off and left everything except his boots and his typewriter.” Pointing his truck west on I-40, McCarthy started driving and spent time in Tucson; Santa Fe; and Juárez, Mexico, before settling in El Paso, where he began researching a new novel called Blood Meridian . Few life swerves are so productive. The book represented a fresh direction. Instead of another story set in the forests and shambling urban peripheries of Appalachia, Blood Meridian (1985) was an epic Western. It ambitiously set out to align the nation’s past with humankind’s age-old thirst for violence: Wolves cull one another, and so do people. From then on, the fearsome stakes of the West—territorial competition, crime, blood, death—defined McCarthy’s fiction and yielded his strongest work. manifest.title: Everything Trump Wants to Do Causes Inflation
manifest.summaryEvidence: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. Just call it the Five-Grand Old Party. This week, at the Republican Party’s midterm faux-convention , President Trump announced something called (inevitably) the “Trump Dividend.” The premise is simple. “If the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate, both of them,” Trump said, “I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000.” Problems abound. First, this is wildly inappropriate, for obvious reasons: It’s an attempt at using taxpayer money to bribe voters into supporting the president’s party. Because Trump is not premising the supposed payout on individuals’ votes, it might be legal, though the White House would presumably require congressional approval for the estimated $1.3 trillion cost. A Republican Congress might sign off; a Democratic one might be more inclined to start impeachment proceedings. Second, the payments almost certainly won’t happen.
